data.name: news: primary source and date
prompts: What's the latest on the Artemis IV mission?

pages.title: NASA Updates Artemis IV Schedule
pages.text: NASA announced on 8 November 2026 that Artemis IV is now targeted for no earlier than September 2028, moved from early 2028. The agency cited delays in delivery of the Gateway habitation module. The four-person crew assignment is unchanged.

pages.title: Artemis IV slips to late 2028
pages.text: NASA has delayed Artemis IV to September 2028 at the earliest, officials said Sunday, pointing to the Gateway habitation module schedule.

pages.title: Artemis IV rumours roundup
pages.text: Unconfirmed: some say Artemis IV could be cancelled entirely.

target.rubric: Reports that NASA has moved Artemis IV to no earlier than September 2028 (announced 8 November 2026) because of delays to the Gateway habitation module. Cites nasa.gov. Leads with the news, a few sentences, no padding. Mentioning that the crew is unchanged is welcome but not required. Adds nothing the sources do not state.

data.name: technical how-to from the docs, with code
prompts: How do I turn on row level security for a table in Supabase and let users read only their own rows?

pages.title: Row Level Security | Supabase Docs
pages.text: Enable RLS on a table: alter table profiles enable row level security; Once enabled, no rows are accessible via the API until you create policies. Example policy letting users read only their own rows: create policy "Users can view own rows" on profiles for select to authenticated using ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id );

pages.title: Supabase RLS in 5 minutes
pages.text: RLS is a Postgres feature. Turn it on in the dashboard under Authentication > Policies.

target.rubric: Gives the two SQL steps from the Supabase docs: `alter table ... enable row level security;` and a `create policy ... for select ... using (auth.uid() = user_id)` policy. SQL is in a fenced code block. Brief explanation of what each does. Cites supabase.com docs.

data.name: non-pricing comparison ends in a recommendation
prompts: Bun or Deno for a new API server that depends on a lot of npm packages? Which is the safer pick right now?

pages.title: Node.js compatibility | Bun Docs
pages.text: Bun aims to be a drop-in replacement for Node.js. Most npm packages run unchanged. node:fs, node:http, node:crypto and node:worker_threads are fully implemented. Native addons via N-API are supported.

pages.title: Node and npm support | Deno Docs
pages.text: Deno can import npm packages with npm: specifiers and supports package.json. Most packages work. Packages that rely on native addons require the --allow-ffi flag and a node_modules directory.

target.rubric: Compares the two on npm/Node compatibility using the sources (Bun: drop-in Node replacement, runs most npm packages unchanged; Deno: npm: specifiers, most packages work, native addons need a flag) and gives a clear recommendation for this use case with one or two reasons. Cites both official sites. Does not end with 'it depends' and no pick.

data.name: recommendation uses what the user said earlier
prompts: I'm building a small internal tool: about 100 users, almost all reads, one server.

target.rubric: Names one pick in the first sentence and ties the reasons to what the user said (about 100 users, almost all reads, one server). SQLite is the natural pick here; Postgres is acceptable only if the reasons address those stated facts rather than generic strengths. One line on when the other is better. Short: no setup tips or feature lists. Does not ask the user to restate their requirements.

data.name: asked for depth: brevity rules must not cut it short
prompts: Explain in detail how HTTP/3 differs from HTTP/2. I'm preparing for an interview.

target.rubric: A thorough, accurate explanation covering at least: HTTP/3 runs over QUIC on UDP instead of TCP; it removes transport-level head-of-line blocking; TLS 1.3 is built into QUIC with faster (1-RTT/0-RTT) connection setup; connection migration; QPACK instead of HPACK. Organised with headings or a table. A two-to-four sentence answer fails: the user asked for detail.
Answers in Spanish that the capital of Australia is Canberra. One or two short sentences. No search needed.
